<Rep. Jared Huffman>: H.R. 2317, the Northern Nevada Economic Development and Conservation Act, is an extensive legislative package aimed at addressing a range of public land issues in Northern Nevada. In total, the bill, as ordered reported, proposes the conveyance of at least 9,500 acres of federal land for various public purposes and would direct the sale or exchange of up to approximately 356,100 acres. In addition to authorizing numerous conveyances and land sales, the bill would designate nearly 150,000 acres of wilderness and release approximately 50,000 acres from wilderness study areas in Douglas and Pershing counties.
Balancing conservation with development on U.S. public lands is a complex challenge that requires careful consideration of both environmental protection and economic growth. Public lands are valuable assets owned by all Americans, and their responsible management involves safeguarding essential ecosystems, wildlife habitats, and cultural heritage, while also encouraging sustainable development that benefits local communities and economies. H.R. 2317 is a genuine effort to strike this balance in Northern Nevada. That is why the bill has received significant local support.
However, H.R. 2317 will significantly impact public lands in northern Nevada, and there are lingering questions about the intent and design of certain details in the version of the bill that the Committee marked up. Most notably, Title V of the bill would authorize the sale of thousands of acres of public lands.
Sec. 512 would even authorize the sale of certain encumbered land to ``the owner of a mining claim, millsite, or tunnel site located on a portion of the encumbered land,'' effectively greenlighting the sale of public land directly to mining companies operating in the area. This would facilitate a broad expansion of mining activity without any federal review or a guarantee of a fair return for the American taxpayer.
The House Committee on Natural Resources plays a critical role in ensuring that federal lands are managed in a fair and equitable manner. Americans do not support the sale or transfer of public lands, and the Committee has a responsibility to fully vet these sweeping land disposals through the regular legislative process, ensure a fair return for taxpayers, and restore a genuine balance between economic development and permanent conservation.\1\ H.R. 2317 should not be an exception this rule. The House should accordingly consider further revisions to the bill or the possibility of advancing the bill as part of a larger, balanced agreement that reflects the interests of the full Nevada delegation.
\1\Vast Majority of Americans Oppose Selling or Closing Public Lands, New Poll and Report Reveal, Trust for Public Land (Apr. 16, 2025), Available online: https://www.tpl.org/media-room/vast-majority-of-americans-oppose-selling-or-closing-public-lands-new-poll-and-report-reveal.
Jared Huffman,
Ranking Member.
